title: The defenseless receiver: why one hit got a safety ejected (and cost Green Bay its top target)
html:
Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this run. It still holds one game file (data/games/gmum7mktl1wy3.json, "Eagles at Bears, Week 3", no snaps logged) and no review files. It was last updated Oct 12. The original football-film-room repo can't be read from this scheduled run (GitHub said access to it "is not enabled for this session"). So there are no new misses of yours to target. This lesson takes a rule from last night's Rams-Packers game, which helped decide the board's Love bet.

The big idea: a receiver trying to catch a pass can't protect himself. The rules call him "defenseless."A defender can still hit him, but not in the head or neck. No leading with the helmet, shoulder or forearm up there.Wednesday, Packers WR Christian Watson went up for a pass before halftime. Rams S Kamren Kinchens hit him high.Kinchens was flagged for unnecessary roughness and ejected. Watson left with a concussion and didn't return.

Letters match the list below. Yellow = the receiver. Blue = the safety.

  1. A · Defenseless. From the moment he reaches for the ball until he has time to turn upfield, the receiver is protected.The same goes for a QB in the act of throwing and a punt returner catching the ball.
  2. B · The safety. His job is to arrive as the ball does and knock it loose. Timing is legal. Aim is the question.
  3. C · Off limits. Head and neck. A hit there with the helmet, shoulder or forearm is a foul, even if the safety arrives on time.
  4. D · Legal. The chest, waist and below. Coaches teach "hit through the ball, below the neck." It can still jar the ball out.
  5. E · The cost. In the NFL: 15 yards and an automatic first down. A flagrant hit can get the defender ejected, like Kinchens.In college it's called targeting: 15 yards and an automatic ejection, checked by replay. In the second half, the player also sits the first half of the next game.

Why it mattered for the bet: Watson had 4 catches, 65 yards and Green Bay's only TD before he left.Without him, the Packers didn't score again. Love finished with 198 yards. The board's "Love: 275+" → NO won by 77.The Rams lost a starting safety, but their run game (Blake Corum, 184 yards) ate the clock (Lesson 50).

In the drill: when a team loses its top receiver mid-game, expect more runs and short throws. Today, Dallas plays without TE Jake Ferguson and WR Jonathan Mingo.

Check yourself: a safety arrives exactly as the ball does and hits the receiver in the chest. The ball pops loose. Foul? (No. On time and below the neck is legal. It's a good play.)

Practice it in Football Camp → (Station 6: Situations)

o: Only after he's down on the ground
While he's reaching to catch the pass
Whenever he's behind the line of scrimmage
quiz.w: From the moment he reaches for the ball until he can protect himself, the receiver can't be hit in the head or neck.

quiz.q: A safety hits a catching receiver in the chest just as the ball arrives. The ball comes loose. What's the call?
quiz.w: On time and below the neck is legal. That's how defenders are taught to knock the ball out.

quiz.q: Kamren Kinchens hit Christian Watson high on Wednesday. What happened?
quiz.w: Unnecessary roughness on a defenseless receiver is 15 yards and an automatic first down. A flagrant hit can mean ejection.

quiz.q: In college football, what does a targeting foul in the second half cost the player?
o: The rest of this game only
The rest of this game and the first half of the next one
quiz.w: Targeting is an automatic ejection, checked by replay. In the second half, the player also sits the first half of the next game.
